claims.text: CrCoNi/NiCoCr can exist as a metastable FCC alloy at ambient and cryogenic temperatures.
The proposed initial metastable FCC alloy contains appreciable chemical short-range order.
Slow annealing enhances chemical short-range order, whereas rapid quenching suppresses it.
Chemical short-range order creates spatial fluctuations in stacking- or shear-fault energies.
Local fault-energy fluctuations persist during successive dislocation passages and provide a strength contribution unique to concentrated alloys.
Local regions with elevated fault energies act as hard motifs that pin dislocations.
Fault-energy heterogeneity forces dislocations into wavy configurations.
Resistance from local fault-energy fluctuations raises the critical stress for dislocation motion.
The heterogeneous fault-energy landscape locally lowers the barrier for deformation twinning.
Twinning can be a primary deformation mode in metastable FCC CrCoNi and related multi-component alloys.
Slow-annealed samples with enhanced short-range order will have higher yield strength than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-annealed samples will show more pronounced dislocation pinning and wavy dislocation paths than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-annealed samples will exhibit a higher frequency of deformation twins than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapid quenching produces a chemically homogeneous random solid solution.
In the random baseline, averaged fault energies provide less strengthening and lead to conventional slip.
The hypothesis applies from cryogenic to moderately elevated temperatures while FCC is retained and slip and twinning dominate.
Using sufficiently low strain rates will minimize dynamic recovery effects.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloys with inherently high stacking-fault energies or dominant intermetallic phase formation.
The magnitude of strengthening and twinning depends on alloy composition and processing details.
